pebbles.title: FloodNet ultrasonic depth sensors (NYC)

narration.short: FloodNet sensors and historical flood events near this address.

provenance.source_name: FloodNet (New York University and The City University of New York)
provenance.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
provenance.citation: FloodNet street flood sensors. Flood events and sensor status read from the FloodNet Data API (api.floodnet.nyc, an early-access beta) at the retrieval time shown. A flood event is a series of depth measurements greater than 10 mm at the sensor (FloodNet's definition); a depth is measured at one point and does not show the depth on every part of the street. Riprap counts the events the API marks as verified by a person. FloodNet's published cautions about a depth: "most FloodNet sensors are mounted over sidewalks and are thus unable to measure floods in the roadbed until the water rises above the height of the curb"; the depth at the street's lowest point differs from the reading by the sensor's height above that point; "a single anomalous data point, measured during a flood event" may exaggerate a maximum depth; and a sensor may miss a flood "if it was offline and awaiting repair or had not been deployed yet or retired" (FloodNet's NYC Open Data description, dataset aq7i-eu5q). Ten rows of FloodNet's deployments table are NOAA and USGS tide gauges (deploy_type "tidal"); Riprap does not count them as FloodNet sensors. Riprap names no sensor, because FloodNet's licence forbids reposting its records: each verified event can be found by its date and depth in FloodNet's own table on NYC Open Data, "FloodNet: Street Flooding Events Measured by FloodNet Sensors" (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/aq7i-eu5q), and on its dashboard (https://dataviz.floodnet.nyc). Cite: Mydlarz et al. (2024), Water Resources Research 60, e2023WR036806, https://doi.org/10.1029/2023WR036806; Silverman et al. (2022), Water Research, 118648, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2022.118648. Licence: FloodNet data and content derived from it are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/), not Riprap's Apache-2.0. Riprap is independent of FloodNet and not endorsed by it.

This is an automated hazard-exposure briefing produced by Riprap from live and precomputed data sources. It is informational only and not a substitute for a professional risk assessment. These are public records about a place, not an assessment of any property or of the people who live there. Riprap computes no score or rating, and records can be missing where people report less.

Place described: 2940, Brighton 3rd Street, Brighton Beach, Brooklyn, Kings County, New York, 11235, United States.

**Answer.**
Riprap computes no score or rating of its own. The Health Department publishes an index for the neighbourhood, quoted here with what it is and is not: The NYC Health Department's Heat Vulnerability Index (2023, from 2016 to 2020 data) scores Brighton Beach, the neighbourhood around this address, at 4 out of 5 [hvi]. The index ranks neighbourhoods against each other: the department says it "uses a statistical model to summarize the most important factors of neighborhood heat risk: surface temperature, green space, home air conditioning, and income". It is not a measurement of heat at an address, and the department says "All neighborhoods have residents at risk for heat illness and death". For Brighton Beach the department's file gives 86.6% of households with air conditioning (a survey estimate it shares across neighbouring neighbourhoods) and 14.1% green space [hvi]. The area is the 2020 Neighborhood Tabulation Area the index is published for, which can carry another name than the neighbourhood in the address above [hvi]. Of who heat harms most, the department writes that Black New Yorkers suffer disproportionate health impacts from heat "due to social and economic disparities", and that "These disparities stem from structural racism, which includes neighborhood disinvestment, racist housing policies, fewer job opportunities and lower pay, and less access to high-quality education and health care" (NYC Health Department, Interactive Heat Vulnerability Index).

**Out of scope.** This briefing does not measure the temperature inside a building, give health advice, or predict the heat on a given day at a given address. Air temperature and an outdoor heat exposure index are mapped on the NYC Urban Heat Portal (https://urbanheat.nyc), by BetaNYC. Where a source was offline at run time, the relevant section omits that signal.

heat_surface.narrative: Landsat measured the surface of the ground within 150 m of this address at 3.0°F warmer than the city's land average, over 17 of the 18 clear summer images (the others did not see enough of this place) from 2023-07-23 to 2026-08-08, each taken at about 11:35 am Eastern Daylight Time; image by image it ran from 0.3°F cooler to 5.0°F warmer. In the latest image, on 2026-08-08, the surface here read 99.9°F against a city average of 97.9°F. This is the temperature of roofs, pavement and treetops seen from orbit on clear late mornings, not the air temperature a person feels.

hvi.narrative: The NYC Health Department's Heat Vulnerability Index (2023, from 2016 to 2020 data) scores Brighton Beach, the neighbourhood around this address, at 4 out of 5. The index ranks neighbourhoods against each other: the department says it "uses a statistical model to summarize the most important factors of neighborhood heat risk: surface temperature, green space, home air conditioning, and income". It is not a measurement of heat at an address, and the department says "All neighborhoods have residents at risk for heat illness and death". For Brighton Beach the department's file gives 86.6% of households with air conditioning (a survey estimate it shares across neighbouring neighbourhoods) and 14.1% green space. The area is the 2020 Neighborhood Tabulation Area the index is published for, which can carry another name than the neighbourhood in the address above. Of who heat harms most, the department writes that Black New Yorkers suffer disproportionate health impacts from heat "due to social and economic disparities", and that "These disparities stem from structural racism, which includes neighborhood disinvestment, racist housing policies, fewer job opportunities and lower pay, and less access to high-quality education and health care" (NYC Health Department, Interactive Heat Vulnerability Index).

heat_visits.narrative: Residents of Brooklyn community district 13 made 48 emergency department visits for heat illness in May to September of 2018 to 2022 (the five-year total), and the NYC Health Department gives an average annual age-adjusted rate of 12.2 per 100,000 residents against 6.0 citywide (from state hospital records). The count and the rate are separate figures in the department's file: for most community districts the count divided by residents and years does not give the printed rate, the file does not say why, and both are printed here as published. Visits are counted by where the patient lives, and only when diagnosed as heat illness.

city_landcover.narrative: New York City's 2017 land cover map (6 inch, from LiDAR and aerial imagery) shows that 82.4% of the ground within 500 m of this address is paved or built over and 17.6% is green (12.8% tree canopy).

landcover.narrative: Experimental: a satellite land-cover model estimates that 83.0% of the ground within 500 m of this address is paved or built over and 16.7% is green (9.1% tree canopy), on Sentinel-2 scenes from 2026; no change between years is read from it. Limits: it estimates the share of each 10 m satellite pixel that is canopy, grass, paving, roof, water or bare ground, learned from the city's 2017 six-inch map, so detail finer than about 30 m is blurred and a tree over a street counts as canopy; against The Nature Conservancy's 2021 six-inch map of the city, on squares it never trained on, it read a typical district's paved share 1.7 points above the map's (at most 7.8 points off in the 46 districts with enough test ground) and its mean error per land-cover group was 4.8 points at best, more than the 3.0 points of the city's 2017 map read as if it were 2021, so the 2017 map is the more accurate source for its year; citywide its maps show 4.2 to 5.0 points less tree canopy than the city's 2017 map in 3 of its 4 yearly maps (2018, 2021, 2026) and 3.2 points more in 1 of its 4 yearly maps (2024), which is the model and its images and not the trees, so its canopy share can be several points off; two images of one summer differ by under 2.0 points in a district's paved share 19 times in 20, but between 2018 and 2024 the shares of 49 of 59 districts differ by more, so its maps of different years are not compared. Rely on the city's 2017 land cover map and The Nature Conservancy's 2021 map (both 6 inch) and the city's building footprints for a survey.
landcover.headline_value: 83.0% paved or built, 16.7% green, 9.1% tree canopy (2026)

heat_obs.narrative: The air at JFK Airport, the nearest weather station (18.2 km away), was 68°F at 13:15 Eastern on 2026-10-05, with 46% humidity and no heat index reported (the station reports one only when it is hot). This is the station's reading, not this address's.

heat_station.narrative: At JFK Airport, the nearest long-record weather station (18.2 km away), the air temperature reached 90°F on 10 days in 2026 through 2026-10-04 and on 15 in 2025; a full year averaged 11 in 1991 to 2020. The highest reading of 2026 was 102°F on 2026-07-02, and the station's record is 104°F, set on 1966-07-03 (records from 1948). These are the station's readings, not this address's.
heat_station.headline_value: 10 days at 90°F or above in 2026 (JFK Airport)

cool_features.narrative: NYC Parks lists spray showers at 7 parks or playgrounds within 800 m of this address (lists updated 2026-10-03 and 2026-09-15, copied 2026-10-05); the six nearest: Grady Playground (spray shower, 307 m), Brighton Playground (spray shower, 520 m), Century Playground (spray shower, 536 m), Coney Island Beach Zone 3A (spray shower, 565 m), Coney Island Beach Zone 2A (spray shower, 710 m), Coney Island Beach Zone 1B (spray shower, 731 m). Spray showers and outdoor pools run in summer only, and the list does not say whether one is working today. Cooling centers are separate: the city opens them only during a heat emergency and lists them then at finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters (or call 311).

nws_heat_alerts.narrative: No active NWS heat advisory, watch or warning at this point, checked 2026-10-05 17:35 UTC.

nws_heat_forecast.narrative: Over the next 7 days the National Weather Service expects daytime highs of 72°F this afternoon, 65°F Tuesday, 68°F Wednesday, 72°F Thursday, 70°F Friday, 69°F Saturday, 66°F Sunday in the 2.5 km grid cell around this place (issued 2026-10-05 09:10 Eastern); the highest apparent temperature it gives, which is the heat index when it is hot, is 72°F on Monday October 5. The Weather Service's New York office issues a Heat Advisory when it expects the heat index to reach 95°F for two days in a row or 100°F at any time, and an Extreme Heat Warning at 105°F for two hours. The Weather Service wrote this for an area; it is not a prediction for a building.

npcc4_heat.narrative: NPCC4 (2024) projects 38 to 62 days a year at or above 90°F in New York City by the 2050s and 46 to 85 by the 2080s, as its middle range (25th to 75th percentile), against 17 a year in 1981-2010 (a baseline that matches Central Park's record, not an airport's); the 90th percentile is 69 days by the 2050s and 108 by the 2080s. Days at or above 95°F go from 4 a year to 14 to 32 by the 2050s and 17 to 54 by the 2080s, and heat waves from 2 a year to 5 to 8 and then 6 to 9. The ranges pool 16 climate models and two emissions scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5), and are for the city as a whole, not for a neighbourhood.
